questions.stem: Which soil type is the most widespread and agriculturally productive in India, covering the entire northern plains and coastal strips?

options.option_text: Alluvial Soil
Black Soil (Regur)
Red Soil
Laterite Soil

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Alluvial soil is the most abundant soil type in India, covering about 43% of the land area. It is primarily deposited by the massive river systems of the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra in the North, and by the deltaic rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) in the South. It is highly fertile, rich in potash, but often deficient in nitrogen and humus.
DECOY BUSTING: Black soil is found in the Deccan plateau (Maharashtra, Gujarat). Red soil covers much of the southern peninsula. Laterite soil is found in areas with high temperature and heavy rainfall (Western Ghats, Meghalaya).
EXAM INSIGHT: Alluvial soil is divided into two types: Khadar (new, lighter colored, more fertile alluvium deposited by annual floods) and Bhangar (older, darker alluvium found on higher terraces, often containing calcareous concretions called 'kankar').
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which soil is characterized by its ability to swell and become sticky when wet, shrink and develop deep wide cracks when dry (self-ploughing capacity), and is exceptionally suited for growing cotton?

options.option_text: Black Soil (Regur)
Laterite Soil
Peaty Soil
Arid/Desert Soil

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Black soil, also known as 'Regur' soil or 'Black Cotton Soil', is formed from the weathering of basaltic rocks (solidified lava) of the Deccan Trap. Its high clay content gives it an extraordinary capacity to retain moisture. During the dry season, it develops deep cracks, which help in the oxygenation of the soil (self-ploughing).
DECOY BUSTING: Laterite soil is poor in nutrients and hardens like a brick when dry (used for building). Peaty soil is highly acidic and organic (found in Kerala backwaters). Desert soil is sandy and saline.
EXAM INSIGHT: Because black soil is incredibly sticky when wet, farmers must plough the fields immediately after the very first monsoon shower; otherwise, the soil becomes too clumpy and heavy to work with tractors.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The characteristic reddish colour of red soils across the Deccan plateau and peninsular India is primarily caused by the presence of which compound?

options.option_text: Manganese dioxide retained in the weathered parent rock
Ferric oxide (Fe₂O₃) released during weathering of crystalline rocks
Aluminium hydroxide concentrated by tropical leaching processes
Titanium oxide derived from erosion of metamorphic rock layers

questions.explanation: B is correct because the red colour of red soils is due to ferric oxide (Fe₂O₃) — iron in the parent rock oxidises during weathering, staining the soil red. Option A is wrong because manganese dioxide produces black or brown pigmentation, not red.

questions.stem: In the classification of alluvial soils of the Indo-Gangetic plain, 'Bhangar' is distinguished from 'Khadar' primarily by which feature?

options.option_text: Bhangar is newer alluvium deposited annually by monsoon flood waters
Bhangar is older alluvium found on higher terraces and contains Kankkar nodules
Bhangar is located in active floodplains and is finer in texture
Bhangar has higher fertility due to more recently deposited mineral content

questions.explanation: B is correct: Bhangar is the older alluvium sitting on higher terraces away from river channels; it contains calcium carbonate concretions called Kankkar. Option A reverses the relationship — Khadar is the newer, more fertile alluvium deposited by annual floods in active floodplains.

questions.stem: The naturally occurring saline soils called 'Reh' or 'Usar' in the Indo-Gangetic plain are primarily formed through which pedogenic process?

options.option_text: Intense leaching of silica and alumina by heavy monsoon rainfall
Capillary rise of saline groundwater followed by surface evaporation
Decomposition of organic matter under prolonged anaerobic conditions
Deposition of wind-blown salt particles from coastal marine sources

questions.explanation: B is correct: in semi-arid plains with shallow saline water tables, capillary action draws water upward and evaporation leaves behind soluble salts (Na, Mg, K chlorides and sulphates), forming Reh. Option A describes laterization, which produces acidic, nutrient-poor soils — the opposite of alkaline Usar.

questions.stem: Despite being poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, and humus, laterite soils support plantation crops like tea and coffee in northeast India and the Western Ghats primarily because of which soil property?

options.option_text: High potassium content from residual weathered basaltic parent material
Acidic pH in the range of 4.5–6.0 that matches these crops' requirements
Superior water-retention capacity due to a vesicular porous structure
Calcium carbonate buffering that prevents toxic aluminium activity

questions.explanation: B is correct: tea thrives at pH 4.5–5.5 and coffee at 5.5–6.5 — both prefer acidic soils, exactly what laterite provides after heavy leaching of bases. Option C is a common trap: laterite is actually porous and drains quickly, which is why it cannot sustain most field crops without irrigation.

questions.stem: Organic-rich peaty and marshy soils formed by the accumulation of partially decomposed plant matter under permanent waterlogging are classically associated with which Indian region?

options.option_text: The semi-arid fringe along the Rajasthan-Gujarat border near the Rann
The coastal backwaters and low-lying fields of Kuttanad in Kerala
The rain-shadow plateau zone of the Eastern Ghats in southern Odisha
The Deccan trap region of Vidarbha in central Maharashtra

questions.explanation: B is correct: Kuttanad (Kerala) — the 'rice bowl below sea level' — has extensive peaty soils formed by centuries of waterlogged decomposition in its backwater polders. Option D (Vidarbha) is the heartland of black/Regur soil, not peaty soil, a classic confusion in exam options.

questions.stem: Calcium carbonate concretions called 'Kankkar' found in Bhangar deposits of the Indo-Gangetic plain are diagnostic of which pedogenic process, and in which soil horizon do they typically accumulate?

options.option_text: Laterization — silica removal; accumulation in the E-horizon under eluviation
Calcification — CaCO₃ precipitation; accumulation in the B-horizon under semi-arid conditions
Gleization — iron reduction under anaerobic conditions; forms in the G-horizon
Salinization — salt concentration by evaporation; accumulation in the surface A-horizon

questions.explanation: B is correct: calcification occurs when seasonal rainfall is insufficient to leach Ca²⁺ downward; calcium carbonate instead precipitates in the B-horizon as nodular Kankkar, typical of sub-humid to semi-arid alluvial zones. Option A (laterization) is the opposite process — it removes calcium and forms in humid tropical conditions.

questions.stem: Under the USDA Soil Taxonomy system adopted by India's NBSS&LUP, the waterlogged organic soils of the Kuttanad backwaters in Kerala — dominated by accumulated plant residues — belong to which soil order?

options.option_text: Inceptisols — young soils with weak horizon development in alluvial settings
Histosols — organic soils with over 40 cm of decomposed plant material
Entisols — azonal soils with virtually no pedogenic horizon differentiation
Vertisols — shrink-swell soils rich in montmorillonite clay minerals

questions.explanation: B is correct: Histosols are defined by a histic epipedon — ≥ 40 cm of organic-matter-rich material (>20–30% organic carbon); Kuttanad's peaty backwater soils meet this threshold. Option C (Entisols) is a common distractor because they also occur in deltaic/alluvial zones, but Entisols are mineral soils with minimal organic accumulation, not peat-forming wetland soils.
